c0676: An LLC separates personal and business liability, which matters when you cook over open flame at other people's events. An S corp election can cut self-employment tax once profit is steady; ask your accountant when it pays off.
c0692: Apply on your state tax agency website. In many states sales tax applies to the whole catering invoice: the paella, staff and rentals, and in some states the service charge. Confirm your state's rule before you quote.
c0700: Bring the Word plan, the Excel projections and written quotes for the van, the paella pans and the burners. SBA 7(a) loans go through participating banks: ask what owner equity they expect and how long approval takes, and do not sign for the van until the loan is approved.
c0701: Have an attorney draft your standard paella catering contract
c0704: Ask for a 25-50% nonrefundable deposit to hold the date (the pricing calculator suggests 50%), a final payment date, cancellation tiers, a guest minimum, a final guest count date, and service charge versus gratuity. Add a wind, rain and burn ban clause: a canopy over the cooking station, induction with smaller pans indoors (rented, not in the example budget), or paella cooked at the commissary and delivered hot. State that the client buys the wine for the sangria, and add photo permission. Reuse it for every event.
c0705: Write your HACCP-based food safety plan for paella, with a written time-as-a-public-health-control procedure
c0708: Cooked rice is a TCS food (B. cereus): serve it at 135 °F (57 °C) or higher, or use time as a public health control for 4 hours with a written procedure, a marked start time and discard (Food Code 3-501.19; ask your county if it allows it). FDA Food Code minimums: 165 °F (74 °C) for chicken, 145 °F (63 °C) for 15 seconds for fish and shellfish, 155 °F (68 °C) for 17 seconds for raw Mexican chorizo (Spanish cured chorizo is ready to eat). Never cool leftover paella for reuse: throw it away. Buy seafood only from approved sources and keep shellstock tags for 90 days (3-203.12).
c0718: Choose a shared commissary kitchen with room for your sofrito, stock and cleaned seafood: hours, cold and dry storage, space for pans and burners
c0721: Visit at least three and ask first: do you allow propane cylinders on site, and where do the pans and burners live? Compare hours, walk-in space and the deposit. A home kitchen is never allowed for catering, and cottage food rules do not cover seafood or cooked rice.
c0725: Your health department asks for it with the permit application. It should name your hours, storage areas for pans, burners and cylinders (if allowed) and cleaning duties; keep a signed copy on file.
c0726: Apply for the county catering / health permit and ask whether you can cook the rice at the event
c0729: Expect an application, a fee, a menu review and an inspection of the commissary and the van. Ask your county directly: can I cook paella on site at a private catered event? Some counties allow it (California calls it limited food preparation, e.g. San Diego County). If not, cook at the commissary and carry the paella hot.
c0734: Check with your fire marshal on propane, cooking tents and wood-fire setups
c0737: Keep the propane station outdoors or under its own cooking canopy, well away from the guest tent. Virginia's fire code, as an example, requires cooking tents at least 20 ft from other tents and LP-gas cylinders outside; your city's rules may differ. Ask about extinguishers and any event or propane permit. Wood-fire cooking only with a permit, and never during a burn ban. Check with your fire marshal.
c0738: Buy a used cargo van and have it inspected by a mechanic
c0741: Check mileage, service records, payload and tires, and read the title for liens. The van is not refrigerated: plan coolers with ice for raw seafood, and shelving for pans, burners and cylinders.
c0742: Title and register the van, and buy commercial auto and inland marine coverage
c0745: Register at your state DMV in the business name. Commercial auto covers the van; inland marine covers pans, burners and gear in transit. A cargo van does not need a CDL (that starts at a GVWR of 26,001 lb or more).
c0746: Upfit the van: shelving, upright cylinder racks, tie-downs and a wrap
c0749: Install racks that hold propane cylinders upright, strapped and ventilated, plus shelving and non-slip liners so loads cannot shift. Add your logo wrap, and check that your insurer covers the upfit.
c0753: Ask for a general liability or BOP policy that does not exclude open flame, in writing. Venues and planners ask for a certificate of insurance (COI) naming them as additional insured; ask your broker for same-day COIs.
c0757: Skip this unless your staff pour wine the client buys for the sangria; you cannot sell alcohol without a license. Offer a non-alcoholic sangria and ask your broker where you stand.
c0761: Required in almost every state once you have employees, including part-time event staff (Texas is the exception: optional there, but venues and lenders often ask for it). Premiums depend on payroll and class code; cooks near open flame may be rated higher.
c0762: Arrange waste, used oil and shell removal with a licensed hauler
c0765: The commissary often handles it. Confirm who removes grease, used oil and trash, and where mussel and clam shells go. Keep shells in sealed, lined bins and take them out the same day.
c0775: Drop-off paella, a live paella party and a full-service live paella event need different equipment. Rent what you use rarely and buy what you use at nearly every event.
c0776: Buy insulated food carriers, coolers and calibrated probe thermometers
c0779: Choose carriers that keep paella at 135 °F (57 °C) or higher for the whole trip, and coolers with ice that keep raw seafood at 41 °F (5 °C) or below. Calibrate thermometers in ice water and keep spares in the van.
c0780: Open accounts with an approved-source seafood supplier and a cash-and-carry
c0783: Buy only from approved sources, such as a seafood distributor, a broadline distributor or Restaurant Depot. Mussels and clams come with the dealer's shellstock tag: keep it for 90 days. Compare delivery minimums and price lists for seafood, chicken and vegetables.
c0788: Stock hotel pans, sheet pans and utensils
c0791: Standardize on hotel pan sizes so everything stacks, travels and fits the carriers. Label pans and lids by dish.
c0792: Set up an importer account for bomba rice, saffron and Spanish pantry items
c0795: Ask for bomba rice, saffron (sold by the gram), smoked paprika, olive oil and stock base from a Spanish food importer. Compare price per quarter, keep a reserve stock for peak season and store rice and saffron dry and sealed.
c0796: Buy your live paella station kit: paddles, ladles, wind guards, work table and canopy
c0799: The cooking in front of guests sells the show. Buy long paddles and ladles, wind guards for the burners, a sturdy work table, a cooking canopy, a floor mat and a fire extinguisher you can reach in seconds.
c0803: Negotiate a caterer rate and standard delivery and collection times. Rentals are billed to the client, so build them into your proposal.
c0807: Use foil pans and lids that survive heat, plus bamboo or plastic plates and flatware for drop-off. Use compostable items where your city requires them, and test that lids do not leak in a moving van. Label each pan with the time it left hot holding and a discard time 4 hours later, or use chafing dishes; ask your county whether it accepts time as a public health control (Food Code 3-501.19).
c0811: Place a logger in each insulated carrier and in the van's cargo area. Save the report after every event as proof that food stayed at 135 °F (57 °C) or higher.
c0816: Run a full test cook for each pan size with your team
c0819: Cook with real rice, stock and propane in each pan size, serve a mock buffet and time every step. Note servings per pan and propane used, then use them to calibrate the kit calculator.
c0825: A buffet needs roughly one team member per 25 guests. One paella chef can run about three pans at once; add a helper from four pans or 80 guests. Write the ratio down and use it to price labor in every quote.
c0846: Get food handler cards for your whole team
c0849: Many states and counties require a food handler card for anyone handling food. Cards are cheap, online and valid for about 2-3 years.
c0850: Train your crew on propane and fire safety: leak checks, extinguishers and shutdown
c0853: Teach everyone to check connections with soapy water, where the extinguishers and the fire blanket are, and how to close the cylinder valves. Name who watches the burners at all times during service.
c0854: Cover OSHA basics: burns, heat, lifting full pans and cylinders, and driving the van
c0857: Train staff on hot pans, heat exposure, lifting full paella pans and cylinders with two people, and safe van driving. Keep an injury log and a first-aid kit in the van and at every event.
c0864: Create your brand, logo, 8 paella menu styles and professional photos
c0867: Offer seafood, chicken & seafood, chicken & chorizo, Valencian, farm vegetable, paella negra, lobster & seafood and easy-eat peeled seafood. Photograph paella cooked live and the golden socarrat; photos sell catering far better than menus.
c0896: Post live paella and event photos on Instagram and social media
c0899: Share photos and short videos of the paella and the socarrat with the client's permission. Use text messages for quick client follow-ups; keep inquiries in your CRM.
c0903: Ask each venue how to join its preferred list. Offer a tasting for the planner; their referrals turn into weekend bookings.
c0911: Cook a live paella tasting for planners, venue managers and corporate event buyers. Ask your local wedding venues when the next bridal show is and reserve a booth early.
c0918: Visit or call the venue 2 weeks out: burner spot, wind, access, water and fire rules
c0921: Look for level ground for the burners, shade and wind, distance from the guest tent, water for handwashing and van access. Ask the venue for its fire rules in writing. Photograph the space.
c0926: Order rice and pantry items, seafood 1-2 days out; prep sofrito, stock and cleaned seafood the day before
c0928: 3-5 days out, then the day before
c0929: Order rice and pantry items with a small buffer, and seafood 1-2 days before with its tags. Prep sofrito, stock and cleaned seafood at the commissary the day before, labeled and chilled, and build one production list with who does what.
c0930: Load the van from the checklist: pans, burners, upright cylinders and coolers
c0933: Check pans, burners, cylinders (upright and strapped), coolers at 41 °F (5 °C) or below with the seafood, equipment and rentals against the list. Record food temperatures when you load and again when you arrive.
c0934: Arrive 2-3 hours early, set up the cooking station away from the guest tent and cook the paella
c0937: Set up the burners outside the guest tent, light them and brief staff. Cook for about 1 hour: chicken to 165 °F (74 °C), seafood to 145 °F (63 °C). Serve at 135 °F (57 °C) or higher, or under time as a public health control, and throw away leftovers. Cook with wood only where your permit and the venue allow it.
c0938: Clean the pans, close the cylinders and return rentals
c0941: Count and inspect rentals before you leave. Clean and oil the pans, close and check the cylinder valves, and return rentals clean by the agreed time to avoid late fees.
c0946: Review rice per guest, guests per pan and food cost against the calculator
c0949: Compare rice per guest, guests per pan, propane per event, food cost and staff hours with what the calculator projected. Small gaps add up quickly across a season.
